title: One idea, three closing moves
statement: Close a lesson with three questions on a single idea: name it, find where it works in the text, then use it beyond the text, as support fades.
example: One design gives the first of three closing questions the most support, the second a frame and the third none.
detail: A closing-questions design that replaces the closing three questions in every lesson is written against a closing section of three unrelated questions that happen to get harder, which it calls a quiz (`grade3-reading/artifacts/feedback-closing-questions-2026-09-24/Closing_Questions_Pattern.txt`). Its three moves walk one idea from being said, to being found in this text, to being used somewhere the child has not read; the finding slots ask when, not what, so the answer shows the mechanism rather than the plot. Support fades because guidance that helps a novice harms once a schema exists, which the design rates well evidenced. Once support has faded it never comes back.
against: It has not been measured with children: an audit found that whether children reach its target success rates, or actually infer, could not be checked from the lesson files (`grade3-reading/artifacts/curriculum-adherence-2026-09-24/CRITIC.md`).

evidence.quote: These are not three questions of increasing difficulty. They are three moves on one idea.
Name it · Find it here · Use it.
The slots must ask when, not what.
Support fades and never returns. Maximum at Q1, a frame at Q2, nothing at Q3.
Say it back: the first of the Grade 9 close questions (mimicry, then application, then evaluation).
the Grade 9 close: mimicry, then evaluation
Mimicry → Apply → Evaluate belongs to the closing questions after independent practice.
1. Mimicry: reproduce a demonstrated reasoning move and explain why it works.
2. Application: select and adapt that move in a different passage or situation.
3. Evaluation: weigh rival interpretations, test evidence, identify limitations and revise a judgment.
This progression is a working design, not a requirement to reteach mastered steps.
Slots ask when, not what; production, never a word bank or tap; at least one slot in the text's own words
The rule mapped onto this text as mechanism, not plot.
A near-miss is plot with no trust in it.
Find it here → Use it, one idea three times, production only, no MCQ/word bank/tap in the closing three, the Q1 sentence recurs at the start of the next part.

evidence.quote: They are a more sophisticated version of the K–8 format, moving from mimicry, to application to the text, to evaluation at the end.
TASK 1 mimicry (the Archivist says the sentence; the student repeats it). TASK 2 apply to the extract. TASK 3 evaluate (""X or Y?"").
